subsystems.name: Core Framework
subsystems.description: This subsystem is the protocol-neutral core that owns routes, blueprints, configuration, request/app context, signals, template loading, and pluggable views. It exists because these behaviors are useful independently of the WSGI Flask object defined in src/flask/app.py; keeping them in sansio modules prevents server-specific concerns from leaking into blueprint registration and configuration. Configuration flows through src/flask/config.py:50 Config and its loader methods, while src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py:376 add_url_rule and src/flask/sansio/app.py:570 register_blueprint are the canonical registration paths. At runtime, src/flask/ctx.py:260 AppContext and src/flask/globals.py proxies make the current app, request, and session visible to views, and src/flask/templating.py renders templates through the Jinja loader. It connects to the WSGI app layer through the Flask subclass in src/flask/app.py and supplies primitives used by cli, json, sessions, testing, and wrappers.

## Overview
The `Blueprint` class in this module (`src/flask/blueprints.py:18`) is the application-facing blueprint object. It builds on the registration machinery in the sansio blueprint layer and adds the file/resource helpers that a blueprint needs once it is registered on a real Flask app.

## Why it exists
The pure registration protocol is transport-independent and lives in the sansio layer, but static file serving and resource access are inherently tied to Flask request/response helpers. Keeping those I/O-enabled methods in `src/flask/blueprints.py` preserves the stable `flask.blueprints.Blueprint` import path while letting the framework's app and blueprint machinery stay separate from the concrete helpers.

## How it works
Initialization happens in `Blueprint.__init__` (`src/flask/blueprints.py:19`), which sets up the blueprint's identity and options before delegating the rest of its state to the parent Scaffold/SansioBlueprint machinery. The blueprint-specific helpers then fill in the behavior needed at request time. `get_send_file_max_age` (`src/flask/blueprints.py:55`) computes the cache lifetime for a static file; `send_static_file` (`src/flask/blueprints.py:82`) is the endpoint-style method that actually serves a file from the blueprint's static folder once the blueprint has been mounted; and `open_resource` (`src/flask/blueprints.py:104`) opens a named resource relative to the blueprint's root path for reading. Actual rule registration such as installing a static route is handled by the parent blueprint machinery, whose `add_url_rule` is at `src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:87`, so this file only adds the request-facing operations on top.

## Key symbols
- `Blueprint` (`src/flask/blueprints.py:18`) — the public blueprint class.
- `__init__` (`src/flask/blueprints.py:19`) — initializes blueprint name/import path/static options.
- `get_send_file_max_age` (`src/flask/blueprints.py:55`) — determines cache max-age for static responses.
- `send_static_file` (`src/flask/blueprints.py:82`) — serves a file out of the blueprint static folder.
- `open_resource` (`src/flask/blueprints.py:104`) — opens a template or data resource from the blueprint package.
- Parent `add_url_rule` (`src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:87`) — the registration entry point inherited from the sansio blueprint.

## Gotchas
Most stateful registration logic for blueprints lives in `src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py`, not in this file. If you are debugging why a blueprint's route was not installed, look at the parent `add_url_rule` and the deferred registration machinery rather than the helpers here. Likewise, `send_static_file` assumes the blueprint was created with a static folder; blueprints without one will fail at the point of serving rather than at construction.

## Overview
`src/flask/config.py` implements Flask's configuration dictionary plus the descriptor used to expose configuration values as attributes. `Config` (`src/flask/config.py:50`) is a `dict` subclass with loaders for files, objects, environment variables, and mappings, while `ConfigAttribute` (`src/flask/config.py:20`) lets framework code define attribute-style access to entries in an app's config.

## Why it exists
Configuration is a distinct concern from app/request lifecycle logic: values come from many sources and need a uniform storage object. Keeping `Config` in its own module also avoids importing the full app object and provides a home for the conversion descriptor used by classes such as Flask and Blueprint without creating circular imports.

## How it works
`ConfigAttribute` stores the target config key name and creates a descriptor: its `__get__` implementation at `src/flask/config.py:35` reads the value from `obj.config`, applies an optional converter, and returns it, while `__set__` at `src/flask/config.py:46` writes assigned values back into `obj.config[self.name]`. `Config.__init__` at `src/flask/config.py:94` records the root path and any default values. Loading methods cover every common source: `from_envvar` (`src/flask/config.py:102`) reads a file path from an environment variable and hands it to `from_pyfile`; `from_prefixed_env` (`src/flask/config.py:126`) walks environment variables with a given prefix and uses `__` as the nested-key separator; `from_pyfile` (`src/flask/config.py:187`) executes a Python file; `from_object` (`src/flask/config.py:218`) imports/supplies an object and copies its configuration attributes; `from_file` (`src/flask/config.py:256`) delegates to a loader callable; and `from_mapping` (`src/flask/config.py:304`) merges a mapping in place. `get_namespace` (`src/flask/config.py:323`) returns a sub-dictionary of keys sharing a prefix, and `__repr__` (`src/flask/config.py:366`) gives the concise config representation for debugging.

## Key symbols
- `ConfigAttribute` (`src/flask/config.py:20`) — attribute descriptor bridging to `config` keys.
- `Config` (`src/flask/config.py:50`) — the configuration dictionary class.
- `from_prefixed_env` (`src/flask/config.py:126`) — imports dotted/nested env configuration.
- `from_object` (`src/flask/config.py:218`) — common loader for modules and setting objects.
- `from_file` (`src/flask/config.py:256`) — general file loader using a callable.
- `get_namespace` (`src/flask/config.py:323`) — prefix-based filtered view over config.

## Gotchas
`from_object` follows Flask's convention and copies only all-uppercase attributes from the source object or module, so lower-case module constants are ignored. The `ConfigAttribute` descriptor has multiple `__get__` declarations at lines 30, 33, and 35; they are typing overloads, and the runtime behavior for instance access is the implementation at line 35.

## Overview
`ctx.py` implements Flask's context machinery. It provides the mutable `g` object (`_AppCtxGlobals`, src/flask/ctx.py:30) and the context object declared at src/flask/ctx.py:260 whose lifecycle stores per-request state such as the matched URL rule and app data. It also exposes helpers used by views and libraries to append cleanup work, copy the current context into callbacks, and test whether a context is active.

## Why it exists
A WSGI process can serve many requests concurrently through threads or async code, so request state cannot live in true globals. This module owns the push/pop protocol and makes `request`, `g`, and `current_app` resolvable per logical context. Keeping it separate from app.py and skeleton modules lets the context proxies in globals.py stay small and testable.

## How it works
`_AppCtxGlobals` translates attribute access into dictionary operations via `__getattr__` (line 53) and the mapping methods `get` (68), `pop` (79), and `setdefault` (93). `after_this_request` at 118 registers a callback to run after the current request is finalized, while `copy_current_request_context` at 154 captures the current context variables beneath a decorator so work that runs later sees the same request/g. `has_request_context` (209) and `has_app_context` (235) ask whether the relevant context variable is set.

The context object's `__init__` starts at 300, and `from_environ` at 340 can build it from a raw WSGI environ. During a request, `match_request` at 405 performs URL matching; `push` at 416 stores a context-var token, and `pop` at 446 restores the previous state and runs teardown. `__enter__` and `__exit__` at 506/510 expose the lifecycle as a `with` statement.

## Key symbols
- `_AppCtxGlobals` (src/flask/ctx.py:30) - mapping/attribute object behind `g`.
- `after_this_request` (118) - registers response-time callbacks before the context pops.
- `copy_current_request_context` (154) - re-binds context vars for callbacks.
- `has_request_context` / `has_app_context` (209 / 235) - cheap active-context checks.
- `AppContext` (260) - the context class containing the lifecycle methods; `push` and `pop` at 416/446 define the active region.

## Gotchas
`push` and `pop` are a strict stack: each `push` stores a token and each `pop` restores it, so unbalanced calls leave the wrong context visible afterwards. Callback-related helpers are safe only when their documented context is live.

## Overview
`src/flask/debughelpers.py` holds developer-facing diagnostics: exceptions and helpers that translate normal request/template failures into actionable error messages. It defines `UnexpectedUnicodeError`, `DebugFilesKeyError`, and `FormDataRoutingRedirect`, along with machinery for attaching a more helpful lookup error to form data and for explaining why a template could not be loaded. It is imported from `app.py`, `templating.py`, and `wrappers.py`, so those core modules need only call a helper instead of building diagnostic text themselves.

## Why it exists
The error messages produced when form files are accessed incorrectly or a template lookup fails are lengthy and purely informational. Keeping them in one module lets request parsing, routing, and Jinja loader code stay clean while still providing rich output during development. The file is effectively a cross-cutting debugging layer over two otherwise unrelated subsystems: form parsing and template loading.

## How it works
`attach_enctype_error_multidict` (src/flask/debughelpers.py:81) creates a `newcls` (src/flask/debughelpers.py:90) subclass of the active form multidict and overrides `__getitem__` (src/flask/debughelpers.py:91). The override first performs the normal lookup; if the key is missing but exists in the uploaded files, it raises `DebugFilesKeyError` (src/flask/debughelpers.py:23), whose `__str__` (src/flask/debughelpers.py:46) renders the explanation. This gives a specific diagnosis for the common case of form fields that are read from the wrong multidict. `FormDataRoutingRedirect` (src/flask/debughelpers.py:50) uses its `__init__` (src/flask/debughelpers.py:57) to turn a routing/form-data problem into an assertion carrying message context. On the template side, `explain_template_loading_attempts` (src/flask/debughelpers.py:124), reachable from the loader path in `src/flask/templating.py:57`, collects per-loader information via `_dump_loader_info` (src/flask/debughelpers.py:107) so the log names each loader and what it searched.

## Key symbols
- `UnexpectedUnicodeError` (src/flask/debughelpers.py:17): small exception type with a distinct identity for unicode-related failures.
- `DebugFilesKeyError` (src/flask/debughelpers.py:23): key error carrying the context needed to explain missing file-form fields; `__str__` formats it at line 46.
- `FormDataRoutingRedirect` (src/flask/debughelpers.py:50): assertion raised for routing situations that would otherwise hide form data; context is built in `__init__` at line 57.
- `attach_enctype_error_multidict` (src/flask/debughelpers.py:81): installs the debug-aware form multidict behavior.
- `newcls` (src/flask/debughelpers.py:90): the dynamically created multidict subclass whose `__getitem__` adds the diagnostic branch.
- `_dump_loader_info` (src/flask/debughelpers.py:107): emits readable descriptions of a template loader's class and path.
- `explain_template_loading_attempts` (src/flask/debughelpers.py:124): turns a list of failed Jinja loader attempts into an explanatory message.

## Overview
This module exposes the context-local names that Flask application code imports as `current_app`, `g`, `request`, and `session`, together with the `app_ctx` proxy for the active application context. Each name is resolved against whatever context is active when it is accessed, so one import location can serve every app and request in the process.

## Why it exists
The identity of the current app and request changes constantly and is only known while a context is active. If these were plain module globals, an import-time value would be stale after a context switch. Keeping proxies in a dedicated file also avoids import cycles: `app.py`, `ctx.py`, `sessions.py`, and `wrappers.py` can agree on these proxy names instead of importing each other's concrete runtime objects.

## How it works
Resolution happens through `_get_current_object` (src/flask/globals.py:18), and attribute forwarding is handled by `__getattr__` (src/flask/globals.py:65), which is why `request.method` or `current_app.config` behaves like ordinary attribute access. The module declares separate proxy classes - `FlaskProxy` (src/flask/globals.py:22), `AppContextProxy` (src/flask/globals.py:24), `_AppCtxGlobalsProxy` (src/flask/globals.py:26), `RequestProxy` (src/flask/globals.py:28), and `SessionMixinProxy` (src/flask/globals.py:30) - so the different domain objects are not all spelled as one generic proxy type. The public names are `app_ctx` (src/flask/globals.py:41), `current_app` (src/flask/globals.py:44), `g` (src/flask/globals.py:47), `request` (src/flask/globals.py:57), and `session` (src/flask/globals.py:60). When no matching context exists, resolution fails with an explanatory runtime error rather than silently returning `None`.

## Key symbols
- `ProxyMixin` (src/flask/globals.py:17) provides shared proxy behavior; `_get_current_object` at src/flask/globals.py:18 is its core resolver.
- `current_app` (src/flask/globals.py:44) is the active `Flask` application object.
- `g` (src/flask/globals.py:47) is the per-request or per-app-context namespace.
- `request` (src/flask/globals.py:57) and `session` (src/flask/globals.py:60) resolve to the current request and its session.

## Gotchas
These proxies are lazy. Storing `current_app` in another global at import time captures only the proxy, not an app, so the value must be read inside an active context. `g` belongs to the app/request context that created it, while `request` and `session` only exist when a request context is present.

## Overview
This module contains the high-level request helpers Flask exposes to applications: URL building, redirects, aborts, flash messages, template-attribute retrieval, and static-file sending. It also holds internal utilities for streaming responses with a live context and for preserving exceptions during cleanup.

## Why it exists
The helpers are framework-level operations that need context state but do not belong in the request-dispatch machinery of `app.py`. Keeping them in one module separates the user-facing utility layer from application/context lifecycle code. It also lets modules such as `cli.py` and the sansio scaffold import the same helpers without importing the full Flask core for every operation.

## How it works
Configuration helpers run first during startup: `get_debug_flag` (src/flask/helpers.py:28) determines debug mode and `get_load_dotenv` (src/flask/helpers.py:36) decides whether dotenv files should be loaded. `stream_with_context` is declared with overloads at src/flask/helpers.py:52 and src/flask/helpers.py:58, with its implementation at src/flask/helpers.py:63. It accepts an existing generator or a generator function; for a function, the internal `decorator` at src/flask/helpers.py:120 wraps it, and the internal `generator` at src/flask/helpers.py:126 drives iteration while keeping the original request context available. This is important for streaming large responses that finish after the view returns.

Response construction is centralized in `make_response` (src/flask/helpers.py:151), which accepts the return shapes Flask views are allowed to produce and normalizes them into a response object. `url_for` (src/flask/helpers.py:200) builds URLs from endpoint names, while `redirect` (src/flask/helpers.py:254) returns a redirect response and `abort` (src/flask/helpers.py:281) raises an HTTP error. User messages are handled by `flash` (src/flask/helpers.py:326), which stores a message in the session, and `get_flashed_messages` (src/flask/helpers.py:360), which retrieves and clears them.

File sending goes through `_prepare_send_file_kwargs` (src/flask/helpers.py:402), then `send_file` (src/flask/helpers.py:417), with `send_from_directory` (src/flask/helpers.py:543) as the common safe-directory entry point. Path setup for locating roots uses `get_root_path` (src/flask/helpers.py:587). Finally, `_CollectErrors` (src/flask/helpers.py:654) is a private context manager whose `__exit__` (src/flask/helpers.py:665) records exceptions and `raise_any` (src/flask/helpers.py:676) later re-raises them, letting cleanup code finish without swallowing the original error.

- `get_debug_flag` (src/flask/helpers.py:28): read debug state from configuration or environment.
- `stream_with_context` (src/flask/helpers.py:63): keep request context alive through a generator stream.
- `make_response` (src/flask/helpers.py:151): convert a view return value into a response.
- `url_for` (src/flask/helpers.py:200): construct URLs from endpoint names.
- `send_file` (src/flask/helpers.py:417) and `send_from_directory` (src/flask/helpers.py:543): send file responses with Flask conventions.
- `_CollectErrors` (src/flask/helpers.py:654): internally defer and re-raise one or more collected exceptions.

## Gotchas
`stream_with_context` is an overloaded decorator; using the wrong call shape means the generator wrapper is not installed and the stream may fail after the request context has been torn down. `flash` also depends on session support, so calling it outside a request context will not work.

## Overview
`src/flask/logging.py` configures the standard-library logger used by a Flask application as `app.logger`. It provides a `wsgi_errors_stream` lookup, a helper that detects whether a logger already has a handler, and `create_logger`, which sets up a default handler only when no user-provided handler exists. Flask's app object delegates its `logger` property to this module so all logging setup stays in one place.

## Why it exists
The logger configuration is needed by every Flask app but is not part of the app's request/routing logic. Separating it into `logging.py` keeps `src/flask/sansio/app.py` focused on application lifecycle and lets the logging concern evolve independently. It also gives tests one small module to reset and exercise when verifying logger behavior.

## How it works
`wsgi_errors_stream` (src/flask/logging.py:16) returns the current WSGI request's `wsgi.errors` stream and falls back to `sys.stderr` when no such stream is available. `has_level_handler` (src/flask/logging.py:31) walks from a logger up through its parent loggers checking whether any handler is configured for the effective level. `create_logger` (src/flask/logging.py:58) is the entry point: it obtains a standard-library logger named after the app, raises the level to `DEBUG` when the app is in debug mode and no level has been set, then checks `has_level_handler`. Only if no handler is already present does it attach the module-level `default_handler` (src/flask/logging.py:52). This means an application or library that configures its own handlers keeps full control and Flask does not add duplicate output. The Flask `logger` property that invokes this function lives at `src/flask/sansio/app.py:440`, and the app name used as the logger name is available at `src/flask/sansio/app.py:423`.

- `create_logger` (src/flask/logging.py:58): creates and configures an app logger, honoring existing handlers and debug mode.

## Overview
This file contains `App` (src/flask/sansio/app.py:59), the transport-independent core of a Flask application. It handles configuration, route and blueprint registration, template registration, teardown hooks, error handler lookup, and URL-building helpers without depending on WSGI or ASGI.

## Why it exists
Historically, Flask's application class was deeply tied to WSGI. By extracting setup and registration logic into a separate sans-I/O class, the framework can keep the concrete `Flask` subclass in `src/flask/app.py` focused on the WSGI/ASGI adapters and let the same core logic serve multiple transports. This is a deliberate separation of protocol concerns.

## How it works
`App.__init__` (src/flask/sansio/app.py:279) initializes the config, instance path, blueprints, Jinja environment options, and default handlers. `_check_setup_finished` (src/flask/sansio/app.py:410) is the guard setup methods call after first request.

Configuration and naming are resolved early: `make_config` (src/flask/sansio/app.py:479), `name` (src/flask/sansio/app.py:423), `logger` (src/flask/sansio/app.py:440), and `jinja_env` (src/flask/sansio/app.py:467). Template loading is prepared through `create_jinja_environment` (src/flask/sansio/app.py:476), `create_global_jinja_loader` (src/flask/sansio/app.py:520), and `select_jinja_autoescape` (src/flask/sansio/app.py:533).

Routing starts with `add_url_rule` (src/flask/sansio/app.py:605), which is the shared path used by `@app.route`, blueprint-inherited rules, and direct route registration. Blueprints are attached by `register_blueprint` (src/flask/sansio/app.py:570), and `iter_blueprints` (src/flask/sansio/app.py:597) exposes the registered blueprints. Template filters, tests, and globals have decorator wrappers plus concrete methods such as `add_template_filter` (src/flask/sansio/app.py:699), `add_template_test` (src/flask/sansio/app.py:756), and `add_template_global` (src/flask/sansio/app.py:810).

Lifecycle and dispatch support live here too: `teardown_appcontext` (src/flask/sansio/app.py:827) registers cleanup callbacks, `shell_context_processor` (src/flask/sansio/app.py:858) builds the `flask shell` namespace, `_find_error_handler` (src/flask/sansio/app.py:868) searches blueprint-local then app-global handlers, `trap_http_exception` (src/flask/sansio/app.py:893) controls whether HTTP exceptions propagate, and `redirect` (src/flask/sansio/app.py:939) creates response redirects. URL defaults are injected by `inject_url_defaults` (src/flask/sansio/app.py:960), with `handle_url_build_error` (src/flask/sansio/app.py:981) converting build failures into useful diagnostics.

## Key symbols
- `App` (src/flask/sansio/app.py:59): the transport-neutral application class.
- `__init__` (src/flask/sansio/app.py:279): default app state and configuration.
- `register_blueprint` (src/flask/sansio/app.py:570): attaches blueprints to the app.
- `add_url_rule` (src/flask/sansio/app.py:605): core route registration.
- `_find_error_handler` (src/flask/sansio/app.py:868): handler lookup across blueprints and app.
- `inject_url_defaults` (src/flask/sansio/app.py:960): supplies defaults during URL building.

## Gotchas
Setup methods mutate shared application state, so `_check_setup_finished` (src/flask/sansio/app.py:410) blocks registration after the first request has started. Code that adds routes late in the life of an app will only discover this when the request handling path calls the guard.

## Overview
This file defines Flask's blueprint machinery in transport-independent form: `BlueprintSetupState` (src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:34) and `Blueprint` (src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:119). A blueprint records route, template, hook, and error-handler declarations, then replays them onto an application when the blueprint is registered.

## Why it exists
Blueprints exist so related routes and resources can be defined together and later attached to one or more apps, often with URL prefixes or subdomains. They are not standalone apps, so a separate module needs to model the delayed application of their declarations. This sans-I/O implementation keeps that deferred-registration logic independent from concrete Flask transport code.

## How it works
`Blueprint.__init__` (src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:174) sets up the blueprint's name, import name, root path, and a list of deferred functions. Setup decorators do not place routes on a routing map immediately; instead they call `record` (src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:224). `record_once` (src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:233) wraps a callback with `wrapper` (src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:240) so it runs only on first registration.

When an app registers the blueprint, `register` (src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:273) builds the state via `make_setup_state` (src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:246) and replays every deferred function with that state. `BlueprintSetupState` carries the target app, blueprint, and registration options; its `__init__` (src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:41) and `add_url_rule` (src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:87) apply endpoint namespacing and rule prefixing. Nested blueprints are supported through `register_blueprint` (src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:256), and `_check_setup_finished` (src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:213) prevents late registration after the blueprint has started setup.

The second half of the `Blueprint` class exposes app-wide registration helpers: `app_template_filter` (src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:450), `app_template_test` (src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:504), and `app_template_global` (src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:562) register into the template environment rather than onto the blueprint's own namespace. Request hooks that affect the whole app are also defined here, including `before_app_request` (src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:614), `after_app_request` (src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:624), `teardown_app_request` (src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:634), and `app_errorhandler` (src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:656).

## Key symbols
- `BlueprintSetupState` (src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:34): registration context passed to deferred functions.
- `Blueprint` (src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:119): deferred route/hook/template container.
- `record` (src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:224): appends a registration callback.
- `record_once` (src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:233): limits a callback to first registration.
- `register` (src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py:273): replays deferred declarations onto an app.

## Gotchas
Errors in blueprint setup often surface only when the blueprint is registered, not at the point where a route decorator is written. Blueprint registrations are stateful; `record_once` plus the first-registration check are what stop callbacks from duplicating when a blueprint is registered on more than one app.

## Overview
`Scaffold` (`src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py:52`) is the sans-I/O base class shared by Flask and Blueprint. It centralizes the route, view function, hook, static-file, and error-handler registration APIs so the two concrete classes do not duplicate that protocol.

## Why it exists
Flask apps and blueprints share a registration interface but have different install targets: an app owns the URL map, while a blueprint defers its rules until it is registered. Putting the shared registration model in `sansio/scaffold.py` keeps those concerns separate from request/response I/O and makes the split between app, blueprint, and transport explicit.

## How it works
The constructor at `src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py:75` establishes the common state such as package/import info and static configuration; package location is derived with `_find_package_path` (`src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py:717`) and `find_package` (`src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py:762`). Many registration methods are wrapped by `setupmethod` (`src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py:42`), which calls `_check_setup_finished` (`src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py:220`) and raises once the owning app is no longer accepting registrations. Routing helpers are built around `_method_route` (`src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py:284`), which supplies the HTTP method list for the shorthand decorators `get`, `post`, `put`, `delete`, `patch`, and `query`. The general `route` decorator (`src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py:344`) returns the inner decorator at line 368; rule options are normalized by `add_url_rule` (`src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py:376`), using `_endpoint_from_view_func` (`src/flask/sansio/scaffold.py:709`) when no endpoint is given. ## Overview
`signals.py` is a definition-only module for the lifecycle signals Flask emits. Each constant from `template_rendered` through `message_flashed` is a Signal object that other modules send to let application code and extensions react without subclassing Flask classes or being imported by them.

## Why it exists
The file separates signal publishers from signal subscribers. Core modules can send an event by importing a named signal from this module, while listeners can connect from anywhere without creating a circular import. This also gives Flask a small, stable event vocabulary that is independent of the internal classes in `app.py`, `ctx.py`, and `templating.py`.

## How it works
There is no logic in this file: it defines the public event names, and nothing else here registers handlers. A consumer module imports a signal object and either calls its `send` method at the right moment or relies on another module to do so. The import list for this file shows the participating modules - `app.py`, `ctx.py`, `helpers.py`, and `templating.py` - which import the signals to emit them during their own operations. Subscribers connect to the same objects, so the coupling is entirely through the names declared here.

The signals cover three areas of the framework lifecycle:

- Template rendering: `template_rendered` (src/flask/signals.py:8) and `before_render_template` (src/flask/signals.py:9) bracket template execution.
- Request and application context lifecycles: `request_started` (src/flask/signals.py:10), `request_finished` (src/flask/signals.py:11), `request_tearing_down` (src/flask/signals.py:12), `got_request_exception` (src/flask/signals.py:13), `appcontext_tearing_down` (src/flask/signals.py:14), `appcontext_pushed` (src/flask/signals.py:15), and `appcontext_popped` (src/flask/signals.py:16) mark context entry, exit, and error events.
- Messaging: `message_flashed` (src/flask/signals.py:17) is emitted when a message is added through the flash mechanism.

## Key symbols
- `template_rendered` (src/flask/signals.py:8): fired after a template has rendered.
- `before_render_template` (src/flask/signals.py:9): fired just before a template render begins.
- `request_started` (src/flask/signals.py:10) / `request_finished` (src/flask/signals.py:11): fire at the bounds of request handling.
- `got_request_exception` (src/flask/signals.py:13): fired when an exception propagates during a request.
- `appcontext_pushed` (src/flask/signals.py:15), `appcontext_popped` (src/flask/signals.py:16), and `appcontext_tearing_down` (src/flask/signals.py:14): fire around application context lifetime.
- `message_flashed` (src/flask/signals.py:17): fired after a flashed message is stored.

## Gotchas
Importing this module creates signal objects but installs no handlers. Handlers only run when application code explicitly calls `connect`, so a signal such as `request_finished` has no effect until a subscriber exists.

## Overview
This module adapts Jinja2 to Flask's application/request model. It defines a Jinja `Environment` subclass (src/flask/templating.py:36), a loader that dispatches among app and blueprint loaders, and the public `render_template`, `render_template_string`, and streaming entry points used by views.

## Why it exists
Jinja2 is template-engine-agnostic; Flask needs to choose loaders per app, collect blueprint template overrides, inject context values from the active request, and emit signals around rendering. Keeping this logic in `templating.py` prevents `app.py` from owning template policy and allows `app.jinja_env` to remain a single customization point.

## How it works
`Environment.__init__` at 42 prepares the Jinja environment so it uses `DispatchingJinjaLoader` (49). That loader's `__init__` at 54 stores the Flask app. Its `get_source` at 57 tries `_get_source_fast` (88) to resolve the template, falling back to `_get_source_explained` (64) when more diagnostic detail is needed. `_iter_loaders` at 98 walks the active request's blueprint hierarchy, so a blueprint template is chosen before an application-level template. `_default_template_ctx_processor` at 21 supplies the per-request template context used by every render.

Rendering starts through `render_template` at 136: it asks the current app's Jinja environment for the named template and passes it to `_render` at 123. `render_template_string` at 151 instead compiles the provided source before calling the same `_render` path. `_render` applies context processors, sends the before/after render signals, and receives the rendered text. For response streaming, `_stream` at 163 drives a template generator chunk by chunk, and `stream_template` / `stream_template_string` at 181 / 200 are the public generator functions.

## Key symbols
- `Environment` (src/flask/templating.py:36) - Flask-aware Jinja environment class.
- `DispatchingJinjaLoader` (49) - resolves templates from blueprint and app loaders.
- `_default_template_ctx_processor` (21) - injects request-derived values into all template contexts.
- `_render` (123) - common render and signal path.
- `render_template` (136) / `render_template_string` (151) - normal template APIs.
- `stream_template` (181) - lazy streaming counterpart.

## Overview
This module centralizes the type aliases Flask uses for annotations across the core framework: response values, header values, callback/hook signatures, error handler signatures, and route callables. It has no request-handling logic.

## Why it exists
The allowed return value of a Flask view is a complex union of strings, bytes, response objects, tuples, and WSGI callables. Expressing that union repeatedly in `app`, `blueprints`, `scaffold`, `views`, and context code would be noisy and easy to get inconsistent. Collecting the aliases here gives the rest of the framework one vocabulary for annotations and lets type checkers and editors report useful errors at library boundaries.

## How it works
At import time, the module evaluates each alias as a Python expression. `ResponseValue` (src/flask/typing.py:12) describes the low-level forms a single response body can take; `HeaderValue` and `HeadersValue` (src/flask/typing.py:26 and src/flask/typing.py:29) describe header inputs. `ResponseReturnValue` (src/flask/typing.py:36) is the common top-level annotation for view functions and combines the body and tuple forms. `ResponseClass` (src/flask/typing.py:47) is used where code is generic over the response class.

Callable aliases encode the decorator APIs. For example, `AfterRequestCallable` (src/flask/typing.py:50), `BeforeRequestCallable` (src/flask/typing.py:55), and `TeardownCallable` (src/flask/typing.py:60) describe request-lifecycle handlers; `TemplateContextProcessorCallable` (src/flask/typing.py:64) covers context processors; and the template filter/test/global callables (src/flask/typing.py:67-69) keep those registrations type-safe. `URLDefaultCallable` and `URLValuePreprocessorCallable` (src/flask/typing.py:70-71) support URL building hooks. Finally, `ErrorHandlerCallable` (src/flask/typing.py:79) types `errorhandler` registrations and `RouteCallable` (src/flask/typing.py:84) is the shape accepted by route decorators and `add_url_rule`.

Because these are static aliases rather than runtime protocols, they impose no checks during normal execution. They are consumed by mypy/pyright and by the imported modules listed for this file: `Flask`/`App`, context objects, blueprints, scaffolds, and class-based views all use them for their public signatures.

## Key symbols
- `ResponseValue` (src/flask/typing.py:12): union of low-level response body types.
- `ResponseReturnValue` (src/flask/typing.py:36): common view-function return annotation.
- `ResponseClass` (src/flask/typing.py:47): generic marker over response subclasses.
- `ErrorHandlerCallable` (src/flask/typing.py:79): error handler registration signature.
- `RouteCallable` (src/flask/typing.py:84): accepted view function shape for routing.

## Overview
This module provides class-based view support. `View` (src/flask/views.py:16) is a base class whose subclasses expose a `dispatch_request` method; `MethodView` (src/flask/views.py:138) extends that idea by dispatching to HTTP-method-specific methods such as `get` and `post`.

## Why it exists
Plain functions are often enough for Flask routes, but class-based views give a home for shared initialization, decorators, inheritance, and per-HTTP-method behavior. Keeping this in a dedicated module separates the view-class protocol from `App.add_url_rule`, so routes can accept both functions and view classes through the same `RouteCallable` type.

## How it works
`View.as_view` (src/flask/views.py:86) converts a view class into a function suitable for a route. Its nested `view` function (src/flask/views.py:106) constructs an instance of the view class and calls `dispatch_request` on it for each request. The base `dispatch_request` (src/flask/views.py:78) is the method subclasses override; it exists to define the contract and is not implemented for the base class.

`MethodView` adds automatic per-method dispatch. `http_method_funcs` (src/flask/views.py:11) lists the recognized handler names. When a subclass is created, `__init_subclass__` (src/flask/views.py:165) scans the MRO for those handler names and computes the set of HTTP methods the view supports, storing it as `methods` on the class unless the class already defines it explicitly. This set is what Flask uses when registering the route, so it can reject or auto-handle the right methods.

When a request reaches a `MethodView`, `dispatch_request` (src/flask/views.py:182) reads the request's HTTP method from the Flask request proxy, looks up the matching lowercase handler on the instance, and calls it with the URL params. If no handler matches, dispatch fails with an assertion, giving a clear message that the method is unimplemented.

The two `view` symbols (src/flask/views.py:106 and src/flask/views.py:115) are both part of `as_view`: the first is the innermost function that instantiates the class, and later code in `as_view` applies decorators and attaches view metadata to the closure before returning it as the registered endpoint function.

## Key symbols
- `View` (src/flask/views.py:16): base class whose subclasses implement `dispatch_request`.
- `View.as_view` (src/flask/views.py:86): classmethod converting a view class into a route function.
- `View.dispatch_request` (src/flask/views.py:78): override point for single-method class views.
- `MethodView` (src/flask/views.py:138): base class for HTTP-method-dispatching views.
- `MethodView.__init_subclass__` (src/flask/views.py:165): infers supported HTTP methods.
- `MethodView.dispatch_request` (src/flask/views.py:182): routes a request to the matching `get`/`post`/etc. method.

## Gotchas
The closure produced by `as_view` creates a new view-class instance per request, so mutable instance attributes are not shared between requests. `MethodView` only discovers HTTP methods present on the class or its bases; a handler added dynamically after class creation will not be reflected in the inferred route `methods` set.

## Overview
`app.py` defines the concrete `Flask` application class (src/flask/app.py:110). It adds WSGI dispatch, request/error handling, response creation, dev-server running, and async adapters on top of the protocol-neutral functionality imported from `flask.sansio.app`. Most integrations and users interact with this class.

## Why it exists
The codebase separates the abstract application definition from the concrete WSGI framework. `sansio/app.py` can define routing and config without committing to an HTTP stack; `app.py` makes those commitments here, wiring Werkzeug request/response objects, Jinja environment, sessions, and JSON providers while still allowing user subclasses.

Exceptions are handled by `handle_exception` (900), `handle_user_exception` (868), and `handle_http_exception` (833). `make_response` at 1227 normalizes view return values of many types, and `url_for` at 1105 builds URLs using the current request's adapter. `ensure_sync` at 1068 and `async_to_sync` at 1082 make async views work by running awaitables through a sync wrapper. `run` at 633 starts the development server, while `test_client` and `test_cli_runner` at 758/816 return the test objects implemented in testing.py.

- `wsgi_app` (1569) - actual WSGI callable.

## Overview
This file implements the click-based command line interface for Flask. It defines the public `flask` group, the `run`, `shell`, and `routes` subcommands, and the module/factory discovery machinery those commands use to find an application.

## Why it exists
The CLI is deliberately separate from the core request/response code so the framework does not have to import click machinery just to serve requests. It also solves a startup problem: commands receive an app import string and only import that app lazily through `ScriptInfo`, which keeps `flask --help` and light commands from executing the user application prematurely.

## How it works
The console script calls `main` (`src/flask/cli.py:1122`), which invokes the `cli` group (`src/flask/cli.py:1110`). `FlaskGroup` (`src/flask/cli.py:531`) customizes click so app state is transportable: `ScriptInfo` stores the chosen import string and `ScriptInfo.load_app` (`src/flask/cli.py:333`) performs the lazy import. During import resolution, `locate_app` (`src/flask/cli.py:241`) chooses an app from the module; `find_best_app` (`src/flask/cli.py:41`) scans for an obvious app or factory when only a module is given, `find_app_by_string` (`src/flask/cli.py:120`) handles `"module:name"` expressions, and `prepare_import` (`src/flask/cli.py:200`) turns a file path into an importable module. Environment handling is also coordinated here: `load_dotenv` (`src/flask/cli.py:698`) loads the `.env` file and `_env_file_callback` (`src/flask/cli.py:493`) handles the `--env-file` option value. The exposed command callbacks are `run_command` (`src/flask/cli.py:935`), `shell_command` (`src/flask/cli.py:1001`), and `routes_command` (`src/flask/cli.py:1061`).

## Key symbols
- `NoAppException` (`src/flask/cli.py:37`) — exception raised when no app can be located.
- `find_best_app` (`src/flask/cli.py:41`) — picks a single app or factory from a scanned module.
- `find_app_by_string` (`src/flask/cli.py:120`) — resolves `module:attr` or factory strings.
- `ScriptInfo.load_app` (`src/flask/cli.py:333`) — returns the app for a command and is the lazy import boundary.
- `FlaskGroup` (`src/flask/cli.py:531`) — click group wiring, dotenv handling, and plugin command loading.
- `get_command` (`src/flask/cli.py:609`) and `list_commands` (`src/flask/cli.py:636`) — handle dynamic command discovery.
- `routes_command` (`src/flask/cli.py:1061`) — prints the loaded app URL map.

## Gotchas
The symbol list shows three entries named `locate_app` at `src/flask/cli.py:230`, `236`, and `241`; the first two are typing overload declarations, and the real body is the one at `241`. Because app loading is lazy, application-level setup that happens at import time will not run until `ScriptInfo.load_app` is invoked.

## Overview
The `flask.json` package entry point is a compatibility layer over Flask's provider-based JSON system. Its five public functions - `dumps` (src/flask/json/__init__.py:13), `dump` (47), `loads` (77), `load` (108), and `jsonify` (138) - preserve the old module-level API while delegating the actual serialization to the active app's JSON provider.

## Why it exists
Flask's JSON behavior used to be configured through module-level defaults. Moving to providers made `app.json` the single configuration point, but old import paths such as `from flask import json` and calls to `flask.json.dumps` still need to work. This file provides that stable public surface without duplicating the provider implementation.

## How it works
Every function follows the same lookup pattern: when an app context exists, call `current_app.json`; otherwise fall back to the default provider. `dumps` at 13 serializes an object to a JSON string, `dump` at 47 writes it to a file-like object, `loads` at 77 parses a JSON string, and `load` at 108 reads and parses from a file-like object. `jsonify` at 138 is the response-oriented helper: it packages positional and keyword arguments into a Flask response rather than returning only text.

The actual implementations live in src/flask/json/provider.py: `dumps` at line 41, `dump` at 49, `loads` at 59, `load` at 67, and `_prepare_response_obj` at 75 are called behind the scenes. This `__init__.py` therefore does little more than route calls correctly, keeping a custom provider installed on `app.json` effective for all of the legacy JSON functions.

## Key symbols
- `dumps` (src/flask/json/__init__.py:13) - serialize a Python object to a JSON string.
- `dump` (47) - serialize to a file-like object.
- `loads` (77) - parse JSON from a string.
- `load` (108) - parse JSON from a file-like object.
- `jsonify` (138) - create a JSON Flask response.
- `DefaultJSONProvider` methods (src/flask/json/provider.py:41, 49, 59, 67, 75) - the concrete serializers this module delegates to.

## Gotchas
Because these functions are only dispatchers, installing a custom JSON provider on `app.json` changes `flask.json` behavior inside an app context, but module-level calls made with no active app still use the default provider.

## Overview
This module defines Flask's pluggable JSON serialization layer. `JSONProvider` (`src/flask/json/provider.py:19`) is the base contract, and `DefaultJSONProvider` (`src/flask/json/provider.py:124`) is the built-in implementation used by an app when no custom provider is configured.

## Why it exists
JSON encoding used to be tied directly to Flask's `json` helpers, making it hard to swap in a different serializer such as one with custom date handling or different C extensions. Moves the serialization contract into a provider object so each `Flask` instance can expose its own serializer while `jsonify` and request parsing keep a stable API.

## How it works
The base `JSONProvider` defines the four file/string primitives `dumps`, `dump`, `loads`, and `load` at `src/flask/json/provider.py:41`, `49`, `59`, and `67`. It also defines `response` (`src/flask/json/provider.py:89`), the method that builds a Flask `Response` from arguments passed to JSON view helpers; before serializing, `_prepare_response_obj` (`src/flask/json/provider.py:75`) normalizes the old flexible calling conventions — a single dict, or positional/keyword values — into one serializable object. `DefaultJSONProvider` supplies the standard-library implementation: `dumps` at `src/flask/json/provider.py:166` and `loads` at `src/flask/json/provider.py:181` wrap Python's `json` module. Its `response` override at `src/flask/json/provider.py:189` produces the JSON response with the correct content type and charset. The module-level `_default` helper at `src/flask/json/provider.py:108` is the fallback conversion used for objects the stock `json` module does not natively know how to serialize.

## Key symbols
- `JSONProvider` (`src/flask/json/provider.py:19`) — abstract-ish base class for all Flask JSON providers.
- `JSONProvider.response` (`src/flask/json/provider.py:89`) — shared response-building path for the base interface.
- `_prepare_response_obj` (`src/flask/json/provider.py:75`) — converts `jsonify` style arguments into a single object.
- `DefaultJSONProvider` (`src/flask/json/provider.py:124`) — default stdlib-`json` based provider.
- `DefaultJSONProvider.dumps` (`src/flask/json/provider.py:166`) — serialization entry point.
- `DefaultJSONProvider.response` (`src/flask/json/provider.py:189`) — builds actual JSON response instances.

## Gotchas
If you subclass `JSONProvider` rather than `DefaultJSONProvider`, you must implement the actual serialization primitives; the base `response` helper only handles argument normalization and then delegates to `self.dumps`. Custom providers are most useful when installed as an instance attribute on the app, so all callers that go through the provider see the same behavior.

## Overview
`src/flask/json/tag.py` implements the tagged-JSON serializer Flask uses for client-side session data. It defines a `TaggedJSONSerializer` (`src/flask/json/tag.py:219`) and a family of `JSONTag` subclasses that encode Python values the JSON format cannot directly express — such as bytes, tuples, `UUID`s, `datetime`s, and `Markup` — as one-key marker objects, and decode those markers back into the original types.

## Why it exists
Flask's public JSON helpers are intentionally normal JSON encoders used for responses and request payloads. Session data, however, has to survive being written into a signed cookie, and applications often store non-JSON Python types there. This file isolates a lossless, extensible session encoding protocol from the public JSON API so ordinary app JSON output is not affected. Keeping it separate also means only the session layer depends on the extra tag classes.

## How it works
Each built-in tag inherits from `JSONTag` (`src/flask/json/tag.py:60`) and implements `check`, which decides whether that tag owns a value, plus transforms for the encode/decode directions. `JSONTag.tag` (`src/flask/json/tag.py:87`) performs the common step of wrapping a transformed value in a marker dictionary. `TaggedJSONSerializer.__init__` (`src/flask/json/tag.py:249`) builds the registry by installing the eight concrete tags defined in this file: `TagDict` (`src/flask/json/tag.py:93`), `PassDict` (`src/flask/json/tag.py:119`), `TagTuple` (`src/flask/json/tag.py:133`), `PassList` (`src/flask/json/tag.py:147`), `TagBytes` (`src/flask/json/tag.py:159`), `TagMarkup` (`src/flask/json/tag.py:173`), `TagUUID` (`src/flask/json/tag.py:191`), and `TagDateTime` (`src/flask/json/tag.py:205`).

`register` (`src/flask/json/tag.py:256`) lets additional tags be added, with control over ordering. During serialization, `tag` (`src/flask/json/tag.py:289`) scans registered tags and applies the first whose `check` matches. The `dumps`/`loads` entry points (`src/flask/json/tag.py:321` and `src/flask/json/tag.py:325`) combine that registry with Flask's JSON helpers in `src/flask/json/__init__.py` (`dumps` at `src/flask/json/__init__.py:13`, `loads` at `src/flask/json/__init__.py:77`) and use `untag`/`_untag_scan` (`src/flask/json/tag.py:297` and `src/flask/json/tag.py:309`) on the way back.

## Key symbols
- `JSONTag` (`src/flask/json/tag.py:60`) — base protocol every tag implements.
- `TaggedJSONSerializer` (`src/flask/json/tag.py:219`) — registry and public serializer.
- `register` (`src/flask/json/tag.py:256`) — adds custom tags and keeps lookups consistent.
- `tag` / `untag` / `_untag_scan` (`src/flask/json/tag.py:289`, `:297`, `:309`) — core encode/decode dispatch.
- `dumps` / `loads` (`src/flask/json/tag.py:321`, `:325`) — small JSON-facing wrappers.

## Gotchas
Tag markers occupy the same namespace as ordinary single-key dictionaries: a one-key dict whose only key is a registered tag key will be treated as a tag when reading a session. Registering a duplicate tag class is also rejected; the behavior is exercised by `tests/test_json_tag.py:32`.

## Overview
This module provides Flask's session layer: a mutable, dict-like session object plus the signed-cookie implementation that stores session data client-side. It also defines the interface used to plug in alternate session backends.

## Why it exists
Flask's session handling is a distinct protocol boundary: application code only mutates a dict-like object, while a session interface decides how that dict is persisted and restored. Keeping that boundary in this module lets apps swap the default signed cookie store for server-side or custom stores without touching request handling. The default implementation is stateless on the server: all data travels inside a cookie signed with the app's secret key.

## How it works
`SecureCookieSession.__init__` (src/flask/sessions.py:73) installs a nested update callback (src/flask/sessions.py:77) on the underlying CallbackDict, so any dict mutation marks the session `modified` and `accessed`. The session interface checks those flags when deciding whether to send a cookie.

`SessionInterface` (src/flask/sessions.py:100) is the extension point. It defines null-session helpers (`make_null_session` at src/flask/sessions.py:150, `is_null_session` at src/flask/sessions.py:162), centralizes cookie-policy getters for name, domain, path, httpOnly, secure, samesite and partitioned (src/flask/sessions.py:171-221), computes expiration with `get_expiration_time` (src/flask/sessions.py:223), and decides whether a cookie should be written at all with `should_set_cookie` (src/flask/sessions.py:233). Its `open_session` and `save_session` methods (src/flask/sessions.py:249 and src/flask/sessions.py:263) raise by default so subclasses must implement them.

`SecureCookieSessionInterface` (src/flask/sessions.py:284) is the default backend. `get_signing_serializer` (src/flask/sessions.py:303) builds a serializer that uses `session_json_serializer` (src/flask/sessions.py:273). `open_session` (src/flask/sessions.py:323) reads the cookie and loads it with the configured permanent-session lifetime as the maximum age, producing a fresh empty session when the value is missing or badly signed. `save_session` (src/flask/sessions.py:337) re-serializes the session and attaches, refreshes, or deletes the response cookie.

## Key symbols
- `SessionMixin` (src/flask/sessions.py:24): exposes the `permanent` flag and default modification bookkeeping.
- `SecureCookieSession` (src/flask/sessions.py:57): CallbackDict-based session whose mutations mark it dirty.
- `NullSession` (src/flask/sessions.py:83): unusable session; `_fail` (src/flask/sessions.py:89) raises on access.
- `SessionInterface` (src/flask/sessions.py:100): cookie-policy helpers plus the open/save contract.
- `SecureCookieSessionInterface` (src/flask/sessions.py:284): signed-cookie open/save behavior used by default.
- `session_json_serializer` (src/flask/sessions.py:273): module-level TaggedJSONSerializer for cookie values.

## Gotchas
The cookie is signed, not encrypted; it may be readable by the client, so it must not carry secrets. Permanent-session expiry is checked while loading the cookie in `open_session` (src/flask/sessions.py:323), not by an immediate cookie max-age alone.

## Overview
`testing.py` provides Flask's official test doubles: `EnvironBuilder` (src/flask/testing.py:27) builds WSGI environments from Flask applications, `FlaskClient` (109) is a Werkzeug test client subclass that knows how to talk to a Flask app and its sessions, and `FlaskCliRunner` (265) runs CLI commands for tests.

## Why it exists
Werkzeug's test client is intentionally app-agnostic. Flask needs environ defaults drawn from app configuration, JSON request bodies serialized with the app's JSON provider, and direct session access. This file keeps that integration out of `app.py`, even though `app.test_client` and `app.test_cli_runner` at src/flask/app.py:758 and 816 instantiate the classes defined here.

## How it works
`EnvironBuilder.__init__` at 49 applies application-derived defaults before delegating to Werkzeug. `json_dumps` at 88 serializes JSON payloads using the app's active JSON settings, and `_get_werkzeug_version` at 100 selects compatibility behavior across Werkzeug versions.

`FlaskClient` is initialized at 125. When a test makes a request, `open` at 204 is the main entry point: `_request_from_builder_args` at 193 normalizes the arguments and `_copy_environ` at 185 copies a base environment, so each request is dispatched through the application with the expected session cookie handling. The client context-manager hooks `__enter__` at 249 and `__exit__` at 255 bracket that lifecycle for tests that want several requests to share context state.

`session_transaction` at 136 is the helper tests use to manipulate the session directly: it creates a temporary request context, yields the session object, and saves session changes back when the block exits. Finally, `FlaskCliRunner` starts at 265; its `__init__` at 271 stores the Flask app and `invoke` at 275 runs a Click command inside the application's CLI/test environment.

- `EnvironBuilder` (src/flask/testing.py:27) - Flask-aware WSGI environment builder.
- `FlaskClient` (109) - request client that wraps Werkzeug's client.
- `session_transaction` (136) - context manager for reading and modifying sessions in tests.
- `open` (204) - builds and dispatches a single request through the app.
- `FlaskCliRunner` (265) - test runner for Click commands.
- `invoke` (275) - executes a CLI command with the app available.

## Overview
This file defines Flask's concrete `Request` (src/flask/wrappers.py:18) and `Response` (src/flask/wrappers.py:222) classes. The request subclass adds Flask-specific routing metadata, configuration-backed size limits, useful JSON parsing errors, and debug-only form diagnostics; the response subclass applies a configurable cookie-size ceiling.

## Why it exists
Werkzeug provides generic WSGI request and response objects with no knowledge of Flask config, routing, or context-local proxying. Flask needs extra behavior at the request/response boundary, so it defines these subclasses in one module. That keeps `app.py` focused on dispatch while the request object itself knows how to interpret Flask configuration and report matched routing information.

## How it works
The `Request` class is constructed per WSGI call and is what view code sees as `request`. Its body and form parsing is inherited from Werkzeug, but Flask inserts a hook in `_load_form_data` (src/flask/wrappers.py:197). In debug mode this attaches a better error object for multipart/form-data problems by delegating to `attach_enctype_error_multidict` (src/flask/debughelpers.py:81).

Request limits are configurable at runtime through paired property getters and setters: `max_content_length` has its getter at src/flask/wrappers.py:60 and setter at src/flask/wrappers.py:89, `max_form_memory_size` at src/flask/wrappers.py:93 and src/flask/wrappers.py:116, and `max_form_parts` at src/flask/wrappers.py:120 and src/flask/wrappers.py:143. Werkzeug asks the request object for these values while parsing, so the properties act as a bridge from Flask configuration to the underlying parser.

After URL matching, the routing layer can record which rule matched. The properties `endpoint` (src/flask/wrappers.py:147), `blueprint` (src/flask/wrappers.py:162), and `blueprints` (src/flask/wrappers.py:181) expose that information to view code, templates, and error handlers. If JSON decoding fails, `on_json_loading_failed` (src/flask/wrappers.py:212) converts the low-level parsing error into a more useful request error.

The `Response` class (src/flask/wrappers.py:222) is the base for responses Flask creates from view return values. `max_cookie_size` is exposed as a property with getter at src/flask/wrappers.py:247 and setter at src/flask/wrappers.py:257 so the cookie-writing layer checks the configured size before serializing cookies.

## Key symbols
- `Request` (src/flask/wrappers.py:18): WSGI request object used throughout Flask.
- `_load_form_data` (src/flask/wrappers.py:197): post-parse hook for form data diagnostics.
- `endpoint` (src/flask/wrappers.py:147) and `blueprint` (src/flask/wrappers.py:162): matched route metadata for the current request.
- `max_content_length` (src/flask/wrappers.py:60), `max_form_memory_size` (src/flask/wrappers.py:93), and `max_form_parts` (src/flask/wrappers.py:120): config-driven parser limits.
- `Response` (src/flask/wrappers.py:222): response class used for regular Flask responses.
- `max_cookie_size` (src/flask/wrappers.py:247): cookie-size limit enforced when writing response cookies.

## Gotchas
The limit properties have both getters and setters, which can be surprising: reads normally reflect Flask configuration, but assigning to them overrides the value on that request or response instance. Before URL matching has completed, the endpoint and blueprint properties have nothing to report and should be treated as optional metadata.

overview.description: Flask is structured as a layered web framework: a protocol-neutral Core Framework handles routing, blueprints, configuration, context, templating, and signals independently of any specific server, while Application Services builds the concrete WSGI Flask object on top of that core with request/response wrappers, sessions, JSON, the CLI, and the testing client. At runtime, the Application Services layer translates WSGI environ data and Click commands into operations on the Core Framework's app context and registration mechanisms, so request lifecycle hooks and template rendering remain server-agnostic. The Sample Applications form a separate cluster that exercises the public API through runnable examples, using app factories and blueprints to demonstrate recommended patterns against the actual framework. The Core Framework supplies the primitives used by Application Services, and both layers are exposed through the package's public API, which the sample applications and related tests validate.

## Overview
This module exposes the context-local names that Flask application code imports as `current_app`, `g`, `request`, and `session`, together with the `app_ctx` proxy for the active application context. Each name is resolved against whatever context is active when it is accessed, so one import location can serve every app and request in the process.

## Why it exists
The identity of the current app and request changes constantly and is only known while a context is active. If these were plain module globals, an import-time value would be stale after a context switch. Keeping proxies in a dedicated file also avoids import cycles: `app.py`, `ctx.py`, `sessions.py`, and `wrappers.py` can agree on these proxy names instead of importing each other's concrete runtime objects.

## How it works
Resolution happens through `_get_current_object` (src/flask/globals.py:18), and attribute forwarding is handled by `__getattr__` (src/flask/globals.py:65), which is why `request.method` or `current_app.config` behaves like ordinary attribute access. The module declares separate proxy classes - `FlaskProxy` (src/flask/globals.py:22), `AppContextProxy` (src/flask/globals.py:24), `_AppCtxGlobalsProxy` (src/flask/globals.py:26), `RequestProxy` (src/flask/globals.py:28), and `SessionMixinProxy` (src/flask/globals.py:30) - so the different domain objects are not all spelled as one generic proxy type. The public names are `app_ctx` (src/flask/globals.py:41), `current_app` (src/flask/globals.py:44), `g` (src/flask/globals.py:47), `request` (src/flask/globals.py:57), and `session` (src/flask/globals.py:60). When no matching context exists, resolution fails with an explanatory runtime error rather than silently returning `None`.

## Key symbols
- `ProxyMixin` (src/flask/globals.py:17) provides shared proxy behavior; `_get_current_object` at src/flask/globals.py:18 is its core resolver.
- `current_app` (src/flask/globals.py:44) is the active `Flask` application object.
- `g` (src/flask/globals.py:47) is the per-request or per-app-context namespace.
- `request` (src/flask/globals.py:57) and `session` (src/flask/globals.py:60) resolve to the current request and its session.

## Gotchas
These proxies are lazy. Storing `current_app` in another global at import time captures only the proxy, not an app, so the value must be read inside an active context. `g` belongs to the app/request context that created it, while `request` and `session` only exist when a request context is present.

## Overview
This module contains the high-level request helpers Flask exposes to applications: URL building, redirects, aborts, flash messages, template-attribute retrieval, and static-file sending. It also holds internal utilities for streaming responses with a live context and for preserving exceptions during cleanup.

## Why it exists
The helpers are framework-level operations that need context state but do not belong in the request-dispatch machinery of `app.py`. Keeping them in one module separates the user-facing utility layer from application/context lifecycle code. It also lets modules such as `cli.py` and the sansio scaffold import the same helpers without importing the full Flask core for every operation.

## How it works
Configuration helpers run first during startup: `get_debug_flag` (src/flask/helpers.py:28) determines debug mode and `get_load_dotenv` (src/flask/helpers.py:36) decides whether dotenv files should be loaded. `stream_with_context` is declared with overloads at src/flask/helpers.py:52 and src/flask/helpers.py:58, with its implementation at src/flask/helpers.py:63. It accepts an existing generator or a generator function; for a function, the internal `decorator` at src/flask/helpers.py:120 wraps it, and the internal `generator` at src/flask/helpers.py:126 drives iteration while keeping the original request context available. This is important for streaming large responses that finish after the view returns.

Response construction is centralized in `make_response` (src/flask/helpers.py:151), which accepts the return shapes Flask views are allowed to produce and normalizes them into a response object. `url_for` (src/flask/helpers.py:200) builds URLs from endpoint names, while `redirect` (src/flask/helpers.py:254) returns a redirect response and `abort` (src/flask/helpers.py:281) raises an HTTP error. User messages are handled by `flash` (src/flask/helpers.py:326), which stores a message in the session, and `get_flashed_messages` (src/flask/helpers.py:360), which retrieves and clears them.

File sending goes through `_prepare_send_file_kwargs` (src/flask/helpers.py:402), then `send_file` (src/flask/helpers.py:417), with `send_from_directory` (src/flask/helpers.py:543) as the common safe-directory entry point. Path setup for locating roots uses `get_root_path` (src/flask/helpers.py:587). Finally, `_CollectErrors` (src/flask/helpers.py:654) is a private context manager whose `__exit__` (src/flask/helpers.py:665) records exceptions and `raise_any` (src/flask/helpers.py:676) later re-raises them, letting cleanup code finish without swallowing the original error.

## Key symbols
- `get_debug_flag` (src/flask/helpers.py:28): read debug state from configuration or environment.
- `stream_with_context` (src/flask/helpers.py:63): keep request context alive through a generator stream.
- `make_response` (src/flask/helpers.py:151): convert a view return value into a response.
- `url_for` (src/flask/helpers.py:200): construct URLs from endpoint names.
- `send_file` (src/flask/helpers.py:417) and `send_from_directory` (src/flask/helpers.py:543): send file responses with Flask conventions.
- `_CollectErrors` (src/flask/helpers.py:654): internally defer and re-raise one or more collected exceptions.

## Gotchas
`stream_with_context` is an overloaded decorator; using the wrong call shape means the generator wrapper is not installed and the stream may fail after the request context has been torn down. `flash` also depends on session support, so calling it outside a request context will not work.

## Overview
`signals.py` is a definition-only module for the lifecycle signals Flask emits. Each constant from `template_rendered` through `message_flashed` is a Signal object that other modules send to let application code and extensions react without subclassing Flask classes or being imported by them.

## Why it exists
The file separates signal publishers from signal subscribers. Core modules can send an event by importing a named signal from this module, while listeners can connect from anywhere without creating a circular import. This also gives Flask a small, stable event vocabulary that is independent of the internal classes in `app.py`, `ctx.py`, and `templating.py`.

## How it works
There is no logic in this file: it defines the public event names, and nothing else here registers handlers. A consumer module imports a signal object and either calls its `send` method at the right moment or relies on another module to do so. The import list for this file shows the participating modules - `app.py`, `ctx.py`, `helpers.py`, and `templating.py` - which import the signals to emit them during their own operations. Subscribers connect to the same objects, so the coupling is entirely through the names declared here.

The signals cover three areas of the framework lifecycle:

- Template rendering: `template_rendered` (src/flask/signals.py:8) and `before_render_template` (src/flask/signals.py:9) bracket template execution.
- Request and application context lifecycles: `request_started` (src/flask/signals.py:10), `request_finished` (src/flask/signals.py:11), `request_tearing_down` (src/flask/signals.py:12), `got_request_exception` (src/flask/signals.py:13), `appcontext_tearing_down` (src/flask/signals.py:14), `appcontext_pushed` (src/flask/signals.py:15), and `appcontext_popped` (src/flask/signals.py:16) mark context entry, exit, and error events.
- Messaging: `message_flashed` (src/flask/signals.py:17) is emitted when a message is added through the flash mechanism.

## Key symbols
- `template_rendered` (src/flask/signals.py:8): fired after a template has rendered.
- `before_render_template` (src/flask/signals.py:9): fired just before a template render begins.
- `request_started` (src/flask/signals.py:10) / `request_finished` (src/flask/signals.py:11): fire at the bounds of request handling.
- `got_request_exception` (src/flask/signals.py:13): fired when an exception propagates during a request.
- `appcontext_pushed` (src/flask/signals.py:15), `appcontext_popped` (src/flask/signals.py:16), and `appcontext_tearing_down` (src/flask/signals.py:14): fire around application context lifetime.
- `message_flashed` (src/flask/signals.py:17): fired after a flashed message is stored.

## Gotchas
Importing this module creates signal objects but installs no handlers. Handlers only run when application code explicitly calls `connect`, so a signal such as `request_finished` has no effect until a subscriber exists.

## Overview
`src/flask/config.py` implements Flask's configuration dictionary plus the descriptor used to expose configuration values as attributes. `Config` (`src/flask/config.py:50`) is a `dict` subclass with loaders for files, objects, environment variables, and mappings, while `ConfigAttribute` (`src/flask/config.py:20`) lets framework code define attribute-style access to entries in an app's config.

Configuration is a distinct concern from app/request lifecycle logic: values come from many sources and need a uniform storage object. - `ConfigAttribute` (`src/flask/config.py:20`) — attribute descriptor bridging to `config` keys.
- `Config` (`src/flask/config.py:50`) — the configuration dictionary class.
- `from_prefixed_env` (`src/flask/config.py:126`) — imports dotted/nested env configuration.

## Overview
This module provides Flask's session layer: a mutable, dict-like session object plus the signed-cookie implementation that stores session data client-side. It also defines the interface used to plug in alternate session backends.

## Why it exists
Flask's session handling is a distinct protocol boundary: application code only mutates a dict-like object, while a session interface decides how that dict is persisted and restored. Keeping that boundary in this module lets apps swap the default signed cookie store for server-side or custom stores without touching request handling. The default implementation is stateless on the server: all data travels inside a cookie signed with the app's secret key.

## How it works
`SecureCookieSession.__init__` (src/flask/sessions.py:73) installs a nested update callback (src/flask/sessions.py:77) on the underlying CallbackDict, so any dict mutation marks the session `modified` and `accessed`. The session interface checks those flags when deciding whether to send a cookie.

`SessionInterface` (src/flask/sessions.py:100) is the extension point. It defines null-session helpers (`make_null_session` at src/flask/sessions.py:150, `is_null_session` at src/flask/sessions.py:162), centralizes cookie-policy getters for name, domain, path, httpOnly, secure, samesite and partitioned (src/flask/sessions.py:171-221), computes expiration with `get_expiration_time` (src/flask/sessions.py:223), and decides whether a cookie should be written at all with `should_set_cookie` (src/flask/sessions.py:233). Its `open_session` and `save_session` methods (src/flask/sessions.py:249 and src/flask/sessions.py:263) raise by default so subclasses must implement them.

`SecureCookieSessionInterface` (src/flask/sessions.py:284) is the default backend. `get_signing_serializer` (src/flask/sessions.py:303) builds a serializer that uses `session_json_serializer` (src/flask/sessions.py:273). `open_session` (src/flask/sessions.py:323) reads the cookie and loads it with the configured permanent-session lifetime as the maximum age, producing a fresh empty session when the value is missing or badly signed. `save_session` (src/flask/sessions.py:337) re-serializes the session and attaches, refreshes, or deletes the response cookie.

## Key symbols
- `SessionMixin` (src/flask/sessions.py:24): exposes the `permanent` flag and default modification bookkeeping.
- `SecureCookieSession` (src/flask/sessions.py:57): CallbackDict-based session whose mutations mark it dirty.
- `NullSession` (src/flask/sessions.py:83): unusable session; `_fail` (src/flask/sessions.py:89) raises on access.
- `SessionInterface` (src/flask/sessions.py:100): cookie-policy helpers plus the open/save contract.
- `SecureCookieSessionInterface` (src/flask/sessions.py:284): signed-cookie open/save behavior used by default.
- `session_json_serializer` (src/flask/sessions.py:273): module-level TaggedJSONSerializer for cookie values.

## Gotchas
The cookie is signed, not encrypted; it may be readable by the client, so it must not carry secrets. Permanent-session expiry is checked while loading the cookie in `open_session` (src/flask/sessions.py:323), not by an immediate cookie max-age alone.

## Overview
This file contains `App` (src/flask/sansio/app.py:59), the transport-independent core of a Flask application. It handles configuration, route and blueprint registration, template registration, teardown hooks, error handler lookup, and URL-building helpers without depending on WSGI or ASGI.

## Why it exists
Historically, Flask's application class was deeply tied to WSGI. By extracting setup and registration logic into a separate sans-I/O class, the framework can keep the concrete `Flask` subclass in `src/flask/app.py` focused on the WSGI/ASGI adapters and let the same core logic serve multiple transports. This is a deliberate separation of protocol concerns.

`App.__init__` (src/flask/sansio/app.py:279) initializes the config, instance path, blueprints, Jinja environment options, and default handlers. `_check_setup_finished` (src/flask/sansio/app.py:410) is the guard setup methods call after first request.

Configuration and naming are resolved early: `make_config` (src/flask/sansio/app.py:479), `name` (src/flask/sansio/app.py:423), `logger` (src/flask/sansio/app.py:440), and `jinja_env` (src/flask/sansio/app.py:467). Routing starts with `add_url_rule` (src/flask/sansio/app.py:605), which is the shared path used by `@app.route`, blueprint-inherited rules, and direct route registration. Blueprints are attached by `register_blueprint` (src/flask/sansio/app.py:570), and `iter_blueprints` (src/flask/sansio/app.py:597) exposes the registered blueprints. - `__init__` (src/flask/sansio/app.py:279): default app state and configuration.
- `register_blueprint` (src/flask/sansio/app.py:570): attaches blueprints to the app.

Setup methods mutate shared application state, so `_check_setup_finished` (src/flask/sansio/app.py:410) blocks registration after the first request has started. Code that adds routes late in the life of an app will only discover this when the request handling path calls the guard.

## Overview
This module centralizes the type aliases Flask uses for annotations across the core framework: response values, header values, callback/hook signatures, error handler signatures, and route callables. It has no request-handling logic.

## Why it exists
The allowed return value of a Flask view is a complex union of strings, bytes, response objects, tuples, and WSGI callables. Expressing that union repeatedly in `app`, `blueprints`, `scaffold`, `views`, and context code would be noisy and easy to get inconsistent. Collecting the aliases here gives the rest of the framework one vocabulary for annotations and lets type checkers and editors report useful errors at library boundaries.

## How it works
At import time, the module evaluates each alias as a Python expression. `ResponseValue` (src/flask/typing.py:12) describes the low-level forms a single response body can take; `HeaderValue` and `HeadersValue` (src/flask/typing.py:26 and src/flask/typing.py:29) describe header inputs. `ResponseReturnValue` (src/flask/typing.py:36) is the common top-level annotation for view functions and combines the body and tuple forms. `ResponseClass` (src/flask/typing.py:47) is used where code is generic over the response class.

Callable aliases encode the decorator APIs. For example, `AfterRequestCallable` (src/flask/typing.py:50), `BeforeRequestCallable` (src/flask/typing.py:55), and `TeardownCallable` (src/flask/typing.py:60) describe request-lifecycle handlers; `TemplateContextProcessorCallable` (src/flask/typing.py:64) covers context processors; and the template filter/test/global callables (src/flask/typing.py:67-69) keep those registrations type-safe. `URLDefaultCallable` and `URLValuePreprocessorCallable` (src/flask/typing.py:70-71) support URL building hooks. Finally, `ErrorHandlerCallable` (src/flask/typing.py:79) types `errorhandler` registrations and `RouteCallable` (src/flask/typing.py:84) is the shape accepted by route decorators and `add_url_rule`.

Because these are static aliases rather than runtime protocols, they impose no checks during normal execution. They are consumed by mypy/pyright and by the imported modules listed for this file: `Flask`/`App`, context objects, blueprints, scaffolds, and class-based views all use them for their public signatures.

## Key symbols
- `ResponseValue` (src/flask/typing.py:12): union of low-level response body types.
- `ResponseReturnValue` (src/flask/typing.py:36): common view-function return annotation.
- `ResponseClass` (src/flask/typing.py:47): generic marker over response subclasses.
- `ErrorHandlerCallable` (src/flask/typing.py:79): error handler registration signature.
- `RouteCallable` (src/flask/typing.py:84): accepted view function shape for routing.
